title: The Muscular System
intro: Muscles produce movement, stabilize body structures and generate heat. Learn how skeletal muscle is organized, how signals trigger contraction, how the three muscle types differ, and how muscles and tendons develop from embryonic tissues.

sections.title: Muscle types and functions

steps.title: Three kinds of muscle tissue
bullets: **Skeletal muscle** attaches to bones through tendons and supports body movement. Its activity is generally under voluntary control.
**Cardiac muscle** forms the heart wall and contracts to pump blood.
**Smooth muscle** contracts in the walls of organs and blood vessels, helping move contents or adjust their diameter.

steps.title: Muscles move, hold and warm the body
bullets: Muscles create movement, but they can also resist movement to maintain posture or keep a vessel's diameter steady.
Normal skeletal-muscle activity releases heat. Rapid repeated contraction and relaxation during shivering adds heat in cold conditions.
Muscle cells respond to chemical or electrical signals, and their contractile machinery produces tension and shortening.

steps.title: Compare contraction patterns
bullets: Skeletal muscle can contract rapidly, but its contractions are less sustainable than those of the other types.
Cardiac muscle has an intermediate contraction speed and can relax during the resting phase of each heartbeat.
Smooth muscle contracts slowly and can sustain tension for long periods, such as when maintaining blood-vessel tone.

steps.title: Additional course details: muscle functions and three tissue types
bullets: Skeletal muscles attach to skeleton for strength and mobility and generate heat; cardiac muscle pumps blood; smooth muscle supplies steady contraction in organs and blood vessels. Control can be voluntary or involuntary.

Muscles produce and resist movement: skeletal muscle maintains posture and smooth muscle maintains vessel diameter. Skeletal-muscle activity produces heat; shivering adds heat through rapid repeated contraction and relaxation. Chemical and electrical signals excite muscle and cause shortening.

boxes.text: The structure and control of each muscle type match its job: skeletal muscle moves the body, cardiac muscle pumps continuously, and smooth muscle regulates hollow organs.
Skeletal: body movement. Cardiac: heart pump. Smooth: organ and vessel walls.
Not all muscle contraction is voluntary. Cardiac and smooth muscle work involuntarily, and skeletal muscle also participates in reflexes.

sections.title: Skeletal muscle from whole muscle to sarcomere

steps.title: Muscles attach and work in groups
bullets: Tendons connect skeletal muscles to bones. The **origin** is the relatively stable attachment; the **insertion** is usually on the bone that moves across a joint.
When a muscle contracts, it pulls the insertion toward the origin.
**Synergists** cooperate in a movement, while **antagonists** produce opposing actions.

steps.title: Layers of organization
bullets: A whole muscle contains bundles called **fascicles**, wrapped in connective tissue.
Each fascicle contains long muscle cells, also called muscle fibres. Their connective-tissue coverings join toward the ends to form tendons.
Muscle fibres contain many **myofibrils**, which are made mostly of repeating actin and myosin filaments.

steps.title: The sarcomere is the repeating unit
bullets: A **sarcomere** is the contractile segment of a myofibril between two Z lines.
Each sarcomere contains thin actin filaments and thick myosin filaments.
The orderly arrangement of these filaments gives skeletal muscle its striped, or striated, appearance.

steps.title: Additional course details: attachments and structural hierarchy
bullets: Muscles in groups attach by tendons. Origin is generally more proximal and attaches to the relatively stationary bone; insertion is generally more distal across a joint and is pulled toward the origin. Synergists produce the same movement; antagonists oppose it.

A whole muscle groups cells with a common origin, insertion, and function. Fascicles are fibre bundles wrapped in fascia; fasciae converge at muscle ends to form tendons. Muscle fibres are long, tube-shaped, variable in length, multinucleate cells packed with myofibrils made mainly of actin and myosin.

Sarcomeres extend between Z lines and contain thick myosin and thin actin. Their parallel alignment creates striations. During contraction filaments move past each other and draw Z lines together without shortening the filaments.

boxes.text: Many sarcomeres arranged end to end let tiny changes in each unit add up to shortening across a whole myofibril and muscle fibre.
Whole muscle → fascicles → muscle fibres → myofibrils → sarcomeres → actin and myosin.
Actin and myosin filaments slide past each other; the filaments themselves do not become shorter.

sections.title: From nerve signal to muscle contraction

steps.title: The signal reaches a muscle fibre
bullets: A motor neuron communicates with a skeletal muscle fibre at the **neuromuscular junction**.
The neuron releases **acetylcholine (ACh)**. ACh binds receptors that open ion channels and start an electrical impulse in the muscle membrane.
The impulse travels into the fibre through **T tubules**.

steps.title: Calcium exposes actin's binding sites
bullets: The electrical impulse prompts the **sarcoplasmic reticulum** to release stored calcium ions (Ca²⁺) into the muscle cell.
Calcium binds to **troponin**, causing the troponin-tropomyosin complex to move away from myosin-binding sites on actin.
Without calcium, those sites remain covered and cross-bridges cannot form.

steps.title: Cross-bridges pull filaments
bullets: An exposed site lets a myosin head bind to actin, forming a **cross-bridge**.
The myosin head bends and pulls the actin filament toward the sarcomere's centre.
Repeated pulls bring the Z lines closer together. Many shortening sarcomeres cause the myofibril and fibre to shorten.

steps.title: Relaxation also needs energy
bullets: When stimulation ends, calcium is moved back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum and the binding sites become covered again.
ATP is needed for myosin to detach from actin as well as for calcium to be pumped back into storage.
Muscle cells replenish ATP using creatine phosphate, glucose breakdown and aerobic metabolism of fuels.

steps.title: Additional course details: excitation, contraction, and ATP
bullets: Motor neurons release acetylcholine at neuromuscular junctions; chemically gated channels open, Na? enters, and an impulse travels along the fibre and into T tubules. The signal releases Ca?? from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the sarcoplasm.

Ca?? binds troponin, shifting tropomyosin and exposing actin sites. Myosin binds actin, forms cross-bridges, bends, and pulls thin filaments toward the sarcomere centre. Repeated cycles shorten sarcomeres and the fibre. Without Ca?? binding sites remain covered; stopping stimulation ends contraction.

Only a little ATP is stored. ATP is required for myosin attachment and detachment and for pumping Ca?? back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Creatine phosphate replenishes ATP; further ATP comes from anaerobic breakdown of glycogen-derived glucose and aerobic metabolism of glucose and circulating fatty acids.

A twitch has a latent period, contraction phase, and relaxation phase. Repeated stimuli before relaxation produce summation and, at high frequency, sustained tetanus. Tetanus infection by *Clostridium tetani* produces tetanospasmin, which blocks inhibitory neurons, causing uncontrolled motor-neuron activity, spasms, and spastic paralysis; immunization prevents infection and treatment can include immunoglobulin.

boxes.text: The nerve signal controls calcium availability. Calcium uncovers actin's binding sites, allowing myosin to pull; removing calcium helps the fibre relax.
Signal → calcium release → troponin shifts tropomyosin → myosin binds and pulls → calcium returns and the fibre relaxes.
ATP is required for relaxation as well as contraction: myosin needs ATP to detach, and calcium pumps use ATP to restore low calcium in the muscle cell.

sections.title: Cardiac and smooth muscle

steps.title: Involuntary activity and cell connections
bullets: Cardiac and smooth muscle contract involuntarily, and some cells can initiate activity without a nerve signal.
Cardiac cells connect at **intercalated discs**. Gap junctions in these discs let electrical activity pass between neighbouring cells.
Smooth muscle cells also use gap junctions. The autonomic nervous system can adjust how strongly both cardiac and smooth muscle contract.

steps.title: Cardiac muscle coordinates a heartbeat
bullets: Cardiac cells contain actin and myosin arranged in sarcomeres, so cardiac muscle is striated.
Pacemaker cells establish the rhythm that coordinates contraction across the heart muscle.
Cardiac muscle relaxes during diastole, the relaxation phase of the cardiac cycle.

steps.title: Smooth muscle sustains tension
bullets: Smooth-muscle actin and myosin are arranged in criss-cross bundles anchored to the cell membrane, rather than in sarcomeres.
This arrangement gives smooth muscle its non-striated appearance.
In the intestine, interstitial cells of Cajal act as pacemaker cells for the smooth-muscle layer.

steps.title: Additional course details: involuntary muscle and contraction properties
bullets: Cardiac and smooth muscle can contract spontaneously without nerve stimulation and are modulated by autonomic innervation. Cardiac intercalated discs contain gap junctions that conduct impulses cell-to-cell. Most smooth muscle has gap junctions and spontaneous activity; trachea and iris are exceptions.

Cardiac sarcomeres make the tissue striated; pacemaker cells set the rhythm and contraction is followed by diastolic relaxation. Smooth-muscle filaments form membrane-anchored criss-cross bundles rather than sarcomeres; intestinal interstitial cells of Cajal act as pacemakers.

Skeletal contractions are fastest and least sustainable; cardiac are moderate in speed and sustainability; smooth are slowest but most sustainable and commonly partly contracted. Slow smooth-muscle contractions help keep ATP use within supply.

boxes.text: Cell-to-cell electrical connections help cardiac muscle coordinate a pump, while slow, durable smooth-muscle tension can regulate organs and vessel diameters.
Cardiac: striated and connected at intercalated discs. Smooth: non-striated and arranged in criss-cross bundles.
Cardiac and smooth muscle are involuntary, but they are not identical: cardiac muscle has sarcomeres and striations; smooth muscle does not.

sections.title: Embryonic origins of muscle and tendons

steps.title: Paraxial mesoderm forms muscle precursors
bullets: Much of the muscular system develops from **paraxial mesoderm**.
Anterior head mesoderm contributes to muscles of the face and skull.
More posterior paraxial mesoderm forms paired blocks called **somites**.

steps.title: Somites divide into skeletal and muscle-forming regions
bullets: A somite's ventral region forms the **sclerotome**, which contributes to the axial skeleton and tendon precursors.
Its dorsal **dermomyotome** gives rise to the dermis and to the **myotome**, which produces skeletal muscle.
The syndetome, a region associated with the sclerotome, develops into tendons in coordination with nearby muscle.

steps.title: Primaxial and abaxial muscle
bullets: The dorsomedial lip of the dermomyotome forms **primaxial** muscle, including deep back and intercostal muscles.
The ventrolateral lip contributes to **abaxial** muscle, including muscles of the ventral body wall and limbs.
Somites form in pairs along the embryo. In humans there are about 38-45 pairs, and Hox gene expression helps establish their regional identities.

steps.title: Additional course details: somites, tendons, and muscle regions
bullets: Paraxial mesoderm forms anterior head mesoderm (face/skull muscles) and posterior somitic mesoderm. Somites are paired transient blocks formed periodically along the dorsal embryo by the clock-wavefront mechanism; humans have about 38?45 pairs. Hox collinearity assigns identities, including cervical vertebrae without ribs and thoracic vertebrae with ribs.

Ventral somite forms sclerotome; dorsal somite forms dermomyotome. Sclerotome contributes axial skeleton and tendon precursors through syndetome. Dermomyotome forms dermis through dermatome and muscle through myotome, including limb, back, and rib-cage musculature.

The syndetome is the dorsal-most sclerotome and is specified by neighbouring myotome; it resolves into anterior and posterior tendon-precursor stripes associated with neighbouring muscle and skeleton.
The dorsomedial dermomyotome lip forms primaxial deep-back and intercostal muscles. The ventrolateral/mediolateral lip forms abaxial ventral-body-wall and limb muscles.

boxes.text: Muscle, tendon and skeleton develop in nearby, coordinated regions. Their shared embryonic organization helps explain how muscle attachments align with the body.
Paraxial mesoderm → somites → dermomyotome → myotome → muscle; sclerotome-associated syndetome → tendons.
Do not confuse sclerotome and dermomyotome: the sclerotome contributes to the axial skeleton and tendons, while the dermomyotome gives rise to muscle and dermis.

quiz.q: When a skeletal muscle contracts, which attachment is generally pulled toward the other?
options: The insertion toward the origin
The origin toward the insertion in every case
The tendon away from both bones
The joint away from the muscle
quiz.why: The origin is the relatively stable attachment; contraction generally pulls the insertion toward it.

quiz.q: Which sequence correctly describes skeletal muscle organization from large to small?
options: Whole muscle, fascicles, fibres, myofibrils, sarcomeres
Sarcomeres, fibres, fascicles, whole muscle, myofibrils
Fibres, whole muscle, sarcomeres, fascicles, myofibrils
Myofibrils, fascicles, sarcomeres, fibres, whole muscle
quiz.why: Fascicles bundle fibres, fibres contain myofibrils, and myofibrils contain sarcomeres.

quiz.q: What happens when calcium binds to troponin in skeletal muscle?
options: The regulatory complex shifts and exposes myosin-binding sites on actin
The actin filaments dissolve
The sarcomere loses its Z lines
Acetylcholine is permanently removed from the body
quiz.why: Calcium binding moves the troponin-tropomyosin complex so myosin can bind actin.

quiz.q: What is a cross-bridge in the sliding-filament mechanism?
options: A myosin head attached to actin
A tendon joining two bones
A calcium store outside the muscle fibre
A gap junction between skeletal muscles
quiz.why: A myosin head binds an exposed actin site to form a cross-bridge.

quiz.q: Which statement about ATP in muscle is correct?
options: It helps myosin detach and powers calcium return to storage
It is needed only to start a muscle, never to relax it
It permanently binds actin to myosin
It replaces calcium in troponin
quiz.why: ATP is used for myosin detachment and for pumping calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

quiz.q: Which muscle tissue is striated and joined by intercalated discs?
options: Cardiac muscle
Smooth muscle
Only tendon tissue
Epithelial tissue
quiz.why: Cardiac cells have sarcomeres and connect at intercalated discs.

quiz.q: Which embryonic region gives rise to the myotome and skeletal muscle?
options: Dermomyotome
Sarcoplasm
Intercalated disc
Sarcoplasmic reticulum
quiz.why: The dermomyotome gives rise to the myotome, which forms skeletal muscle.

quiz.q: Which is an example of primaxial muscle described in the unit?
options: Deep muscles of the back
Muscle in the ventral body wall only
The heart's pacemaker cells
Smooth muscle in the intestine
quiz.why: Primaxial muscle includes deep back and intercostal muscles.
